newsitem.title: CHINA: No rest on North Korea defector crisis seventh day.
newsitem.headline: No rest on North Korea defector crisis seventh day.

text.p: The most senior leader to flee North Korea spent his seventh day at the centre of a diplomatic crisis on Tuesday, despite an apparent softening in Pyongyang's hardline stance on his defection.

South Korean officials said talks continued with Beijing over the fate of Hwang Jang-yop, a top aide to supreme North Korean leader Kim Jong-il, who has been stranded in Seoul's Beijing mission since he sought refuge there last Wednesday.

Chinese security forces sent three armoured personnel carriers to guard approaches to the mission, apparently not reassured by signs Pyongyang could be coming to terms with the loss of one of its greatest ideological thinkers.
The official KCNA news agency said late on Monday that North Korea would take strong action if it turned out that Hwang was kidnapped, but that he would be fired if he had sought asylum.
"Our stand is simple and clear. If he was kidnapped, we cannot tolerate it and we will take decisive countermeasures," the agency quoted the North Korean Foreign Ministry as saying.
"If he sought asylum, it means that he is a renegade and he is dismissed," the ministry said, adding that it had asked Beijing to investigate what it called Hwang's disappearance.

Pyongyang officials had previously been steadfast in their accusation that Seoul abducted the scholarly architect of North Korea's governing ideology of Juche, or strict self-reliance. South Korea has dismissed the charge as preposterous.

The new tone on Hwang's departure appeared to be backed by comments by North Korean leader Kim Jong-il broadcast on state radio that those who lacked the grit to defend Pyongyang's fiery brand of communism should go their own way.

"As the revolutionary song goes: Cowards, Leave If You Want To! We will defend the red flag to the bitter end. We will move forward by holding the Juche banner even higher," a political essay broadcast by state radio quoted Kim as saying.

South Korean officials said the new tone from the North, whose officials had earlier issued threats of war and violence if Hwang was compelled to go to Seoul, meant Pyongyang had reconsidered its stance.

North Korean officials, who had kept vigil outside South Korea's Beijing mission since the beginning of the crisis, largely withdrew from the area on Tuesday but the move failed to stop China boosting security in the sedate diplomatic quarter.
Beijing, an unwilling third party in the feuding between the two hostile sides on the Korean peninsula, on Tuesday repeated its plea to both to act with restraint to resolve the affair.

The stationing of white armoured personnel carriers along the tree-lined approaches to the South Korean mission bolstered the visible defences that already included scores of regular and paramilitary police armed with assault rifles.
A crowd control truck armed with water cannon and a bullet-proof car have been parked outside the mission for days.
Passing Beijing residents, many of them previously unaware of a diplomatic drama ignored by China's state media, clustered beyond the police cordon for a glimpse of the mission.
"I think this one North Korean guy has made a lot of trouble for China," said one Beijing worker who came to watch after hearing about Hwang's defection on foreign shortwave radio.
"This is not a comfortable situation for the Chinese government," he said.
